source.title: MERIT: Maximum-normalized Element-wise Ratio for Language Model Large-batch Training
source.authors: Yang Luo; Zangwei Zheng; Zi-Heng Qin; Zi-Rui Zhu; Yong Liu; Yang You

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the full paper and appendices. Some figure values are not provided as text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether large-batch training harms held-out performance and whether a changed optimizer recipe can reduce that penalty, using language-model training and evaluation results.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports attention-logit and Hessian measurements, but these do not directly measure the training-to-test gap or V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure. Other optimizers' results are included only where they provide a comparison for the large-batch setting.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5's recipe-adaptation clause by comparing large-batch MERIT with small-batch AdamW at the same 48B-token budget. It also explicitly reports AdamW degradation as batch size increases. The token-matched comparison changes optimizer, so it does not isolate batch size.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that MERIT enables larger GPT training batches while maintaining comparable generalization, and improves validation loss and downstream results against the tested large-batch optimizer baselines. Comparable performance in the 48B-token comparison concerns the task average, not every individual task.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces MERIT, a max-norm and element-wise trust-ratio optimizer with element-wise clipping, and compares it with AdamW and LAMB.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported large-batch performance varies with optimizer and model size. The paper also states that AdamW's large-batch degradation requires additional training tokens to reach comparable generalization levels.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed large batch sizes, MERIT achieves lower validation loss than AdamW and LAMB on GPT-2 and Llama models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice affects held-out performance during large-batch language-model training. These comparisons alone establish neither a batch-size penalty nor an adaptive-versus-SGD difference.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-2 Small trained with MERIT has a Hessian top eigenvalue of 12.326 and trace of 3444.92, versus 37.231 and 12994.91 with AdamW.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MERIT reaches a point with lower Hessian curvature than AdamW in this comparison; this does not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or training–test gap.

fits_no_version.finding: MERIT reduces attention-logit spikes, especially in middle layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimizer changes attention-logit dynamics during large-batch training; attention logits alone do not measure any listed generalization claim.

record.problems: The main same-token large-batch comparison changes the optimizer, so the batch-size effect is not isolated. The equal-step validation-loss claims are primarily presented in figures; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors note that the evaluated models are modest in size and that broader downstream assessment is limited.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Figure 1 describes batch-size scaling and AdamW degradation but does not provide recoverable numeric results in the supplied text; Table 1 provides the explicit same-token comparison extracted here.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD, including sensitivity to tuning breadth.

Image-classification settings and isolated effects of longer training, learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or regularization. The 48B-token comparison does not separate the optimizer change from the batch-size change.
Effects of adding dropout or removing dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its relationship to measured training–test gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

missing.what: Task-level results qualify the apparent preservation of performance in R1. For GPT-2 Small, AdamW→MERIT scores are ARC 43.43→45.83, COPA 66.00→67.00, HellaSwag 29.20→28.82, RACE 29.00→27.56, and WIC 50.16→50.16. The higher average conceals lower scores on two tasks.

Task-level results qualify R2. For GPT-2 Medium, AdamW→MERIT scores are ARC 49.49→50.38, COPA 71.00→70.00, HellaSwag 32.39→32.32, RACE 30.05→30.33, and WIC 50.00→50.47. The higher average conceals lower scores on two tasks.

record.verdict_notes: No uncertainty estimates establish equivalence or significant superiority. The AdamW batch-scaling results in Figure 1 are already declared in rows_left_out; their plotted values cannot be recovered from the supplied text. R1–R2 support the adaptation clause of V5, not an unconditional claim that larger batches preserve performance.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD under different tuning regimes.

The study does not isolate batch-size effects under a fixed optimizer and otherwise unchanged recipe across a broad batch-size sweep; its principal same-token comparison changes the optimizer, and its training-loss-equivalent comparison is figure-based.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.
